extracted.intended_audience: geologists, geognosists, advanced students of physical geography and volcanology
extracted.subtask_description: Framework for classifying rocks by mode of origin and for characterizing volcanic phenomena and stages (including diagnostic products, geomorphological types, and relations to sea water). Intended as guidance for geological description and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four modes of rock origin
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Rocks admit of being arranged according to four modes of origin.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The four modes are: (1) 'Rocks of eruption' (issued from the interior by volcanic or plutonic action), (2) 'Sedimentary rocks' (precipitated/deposited from a fluid), (3) 'Transformed or metamorphic rocks' (texture and stratification changed by internal agencies), and (4) 'Conglomerates' (mechanically-derived breccias/sandstones). Use these formative processes rather than solely external form/superposition for classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rocks of eruption (endogenous/erupted rocks)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Rocks of eruption', which have issued from the interior of the earth either in a state of fusion from volcanic action, or in a more or less soft, viscous condition, from Plutonic action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as endogenous (or 'nether-formed' / 'hypogene') rocks; recognize them by mode of origin and by mineralogical/structural features. They are commonly compact and abnormal and include groups such as granite, syenite, porphyries, basalts, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sedimentary rocks (exogenous)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Sedimentary rocks', which have been precipitated and deposited on the earth's surface from a fluid, in which the most minute particles were either dissolved or held in suspension constituting the greater part of the secondary (or flotz) and tertiary groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify deposits formed by precipitation/accumulation from water (e.g., travertine, marine limestones). Note that recent sea-formed deposits may already entomb human artifacts; observe textural and fossil evidence to infer depositional environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformed or metamorphic rocks
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Transformed or metamorphic rocks', in which the internal texture and the mode of stratification have been changed, either by contact or proximity with a Plutonic or volcanic endogenous rock of eruption, or by gaseous sublimation of substances which accompany certain masses erupted in a hot, fluid condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metamorphism as a diagnostic category: in the wide sense include any post-depositional change of aggregation, structure, or chemical condition; in the narrower sense restrict to changes produced by interior agencies. Look for contact effects, alteration of minerals, discoloration, formation of new minerals (e.g., conversion of anhydrite to gypsum), and infer processes (thermal, electro-chemical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conglomerates (mechanical accumulations)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Conglomerates'; coarse or finely granular sandstones, or breccias composed of mechanically-divided masses of the three previous species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify coarse mechanically-derived rocks (breccia, conglomerate) by clast composition and provenance (derived from erupted, sedimentary, or metamorphic sources) and by cementation processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stages of volcanic activity diagnosed by emitted products
rubrics_metrics.description: Every stage of volcanic activity, from its first origin to its extinction, is characterized by peculiar products: first ignited scoriae, lava streams (trachyte, pyroxene, obsidian), rapilli and tufaceous ashes with large quantities of pure aqueous vapor; subsequently, solfatara stage with aqueous vapors mixed with sulphureted hydrogen and carbonic acid gases; finally, cooled stage with exhalations of carbonic acid alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the character of erupted materials and gas composition to infer the stage of activity. Presence of lava and scoriae indicates active eruptive stage; sulphureted hydrogen/carbonic acid mixtures indicate solfatara/degassing stage; only CO2 exhalations indicate cooled/extinct stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of igneous mountains that emit no lava (mud/water/sulphur eruptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a remarkable class of igneous mountains which do not eject lava, but merely devastating streams of hot water impregnated with burning sulphur and rocks reduced to a state of dust (e.g., Galungung in Java).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume absence of lava implies non-volcanic origin; treat these as possible normal or transitory forms of volcanic activity. Field chemical analyses and observation of eruption products are needed to interpret whether they represent a distinct mode or a transient phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the role of sea proximity and penetration of sea water in volcanic activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses exist that penetration of sea water into volcanic foci explains the necessity of vicinity to the sea; evidence includes aqueous vapors from volcanoes, presence of chlorides, hydrochloric acid in fumaroles, and historical accounts linking littoral sites to persistent activity. Counter-evidence: many active volcanoes lie far inland (hundreds to over a thousand miles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether sea or meteoric water has access to foci by examining gas chemistry (chlorides, HCl), aqueous vapor volumes, hydrostatic pressure considerations (compare vapor pressure vs seawater pressure at depth), closure of channels, and the geographic/historical distribution of volcanism. Use multiple lines of evidence rather than assuming a single causal relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of geographic distribution and distance-from-sea data in interpreting volcanic origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographic distribution of historically active volcanoes and many insular/littoral volcanic mountains led to belief that volcanic activity connected with the sea; yet some active volcanoes (e.g., in Central Asia) lie very far from the ocean, showing sea proximity is not absolutely necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In interpreting volcanic causes, compile distances to nearest seas, local basin depth, and palaeogeography (former seas/lakes). Consider whether littoral settings merely favor eruption by offering margins of deep sea-basins that reduce resistance, and weigh this against inland volcanic occurrences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for identifying 'craters of elevation' and island-formation mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Islands like Santorino combine characteristics of islands of elevation: an outer wall (older islands) with central later-formed islands (Neokaimeni, Microkaimeni) produced partly by upheaved seabed and partly by erupted matter (often erupted beneath water).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bathymetric soundings, stratigraphic relations (volcanic strata abutting limestone), composition (obsidian, pumice, scoria), stratification of pumiceous ash, and ongoing submarine fumarolic activity to infer crater-of-elevation vs purely eruptive island origin. Observe temporal emergence/subsidence history of submarine cones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and documentation of ephemeral submarine islands
rubrics_metrics.description: Submarine islands sometimes appear and disappear (e.g., Sabrina, Ferdinandea); such islands may be ephemeral and require timely scientific attention and documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a new submarine island arises, promptly record observations (soundings, composition, dimensions, permanence). Historical examples show political/maritime events can prevent early study; timely publication and measurement are important for scientific record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endogenous vs exogenous nomenclature and mapping conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal to term plutonic/volcanic eruptive rocks 'endogenous' (generated in the interior) and sedimentary/flotz rocks 'exogenous' (generated externally); use graphic symbols to indicate ascent or deposition directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt clear nomenclature and map symbols (author's pasigraphic plan) to represent genesis (endogenous/exogenous) and directional relations; align with existing nomenclature (e.g., De Candolle) but note terminological caveats from botany analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granite and syenite diagnostic features and relations
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Granite and syenite' of different ages; granite often traverses syenite in veins and can be more recent, forming ellipsoidal masses covered by a shell cleft into blocks; granite may occur as ledges, concentric scaling, flattened spherical masses, and can superpose on older rocks (slate, Jura limestone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify granite by morphology (insulated ellipsoidal masses, concentric scaling, ledges), mineralogy (feldspar, albite, titaniferous crystals), and relations (veining through syenite, superposition on older strata). Use regional examples (Altai, Ural, Orinoco cataracts, Papagallo) as analogues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quartzose porphyry characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Quartzose porphyry' often occurs in the relation of veins to other rocks; the base is generally a finely granular mixture of the same elements which occur in the larger imbedded crystals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize by porphyritic texture: larger embedded crystals in a fine-grained feldspathic/quartz base. Note variations (e.g., granitic porphyry poor in quartz with granular/layered feldspathic base) and relation to host rocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greenstones and diorite description
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Greenstones, Diorite' are granular mixtures of white albite and blackish-green hornblende, forming dioritic porphyry when the crystals are deposited in a base of denser tissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose by mineral assemblage (albite + hornblende), texture (granular, porphyritic where crystals are set in denser matrix), and consider field occurrences when assigning to greenstone/diorite groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite rocks and their diagnostic significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite rocks are definite associations of certain cryptonostic simple minerals, as feldspar, mica, solid silex, augite, and nepheline; similar composites are formed by volcanic processes and recur across distant zones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mineralogical composition and grouping patterns (not only gross rock type) to recognize composite rocks; expect repetition of minute characteristics across latitudes — use these as diagnostic markers in correlation and mapping.
